status: draft from snapshot of 2026-11-15; needs review by someone who knows the work
position: Assistant Professor, Khoury College of Computer Sciences, Northeastern; directs the PEACH (Privacy-Enabling AI and Computer-Human interaction) Lab; core faculty, Cybersecurity and Privacy Institute
training: PhD in HCI, Carnegie Mellon; BS in CS, Peking University; postdoc at UC Berkeley; worked at Google

current_focus.summary: Emerging LLM privacy issues studied from a human-centered perspective: privacy is framed as sustaining human agency, safe exploration, and free expression.

threads.name: Data minimization in LLM systems
evidence: 'It's a Fair Game', or Is It? (CHI'24): users' disclosure risk–benefit trade-offs and erroneous mental models in LLM chatbots
Rescriber (CHI'25): user-led data minimization browser extension
Operationalizing Data Minimization for Privacy-Preserving LLM Prompting (ICLR'26)

threads.name: Human oversight and control of agentic AI
evidence: Dark Patterns Meet GUI Agents (CHI'26)
GUI agents and fine-print injections (TAISAP'26)
Ongoing: human oversight of privacy leakage in LLM agents; comparing oversight strategies for computer-use agents

threads.name: Personalization, autonomy, and contextual integrity in AI agents
evidence: PrivacyLens (NeurIPS'24 D&B): privacy norm awareness of LLM agents
Autonomy Reshapes How Personalization Affects Privacy Concerns and Trust in LLM Agents (COLM'26): risk-contingent autonomy improves perceived control
CIDER (COLM'26): contextual disclosure boundaries for privacy preference alignment
AuthorizationBench (preprint, 2026): agents acting beyond the user's authorization

threads.name: Epistemic trust and surveillance power: inference and re-identification
evidence: Position papers (2025; NeurIPS'26 Position Track): LLM privacy is lifecycle-wide; inference-time context leakage, agent behavior, and data aggregation are understudied vs memorization
Agentic LLMs as deanonymizers: re-identification of participants in an interview dataset (preprint, Jan 2026)
AgentDoxx (preprint, 2026): agentic re-identification of anonymized interview transcripts with web search
Secret Use of LLMs (CSCW'25)

threads.name: AI to support privacy management and design
evidence: Human-as-the-unit privacy management with AI agents (CHI'26)
PrivacyMotiv (DIS'26): LLM-generated persona journeys to motivate privacy reviews by UX practitioners
Ongoing: privacy controls in interview chatbots

current_focus.methods: Mixed methods: interviews, surveys, large experiments (e.g., N=450), plus building systems, datasets, and benchmarks.

older_work.summary: Usable privacy for mobile app developers (PhD and postdoc era, ~2018–2024).
evidence: Coconut (IMWUT 2018): IDE plugin for privacy-friendly Android apps
Honeysuckle (IMWUT 2021): annotation-guided in-app privacy notices
Developer privacy discussions on Reddit (CSCW 2021)
COVID-19 contact-tracing app adoption survey experiment (PMC 2021)
Privacy nutrition labels: developer challenges (CHI'22, Best Paper HM); Matcha IDE plugin (IMWUT 2024)
older_work.trap_note: The official Khoury profile biography still describes this era (IDE plugins, enabling non-specialist developers). Presenting developer tools or privacy labels as Prof. Li's current focus is an R2 'older work as current' violation.

misdescription_examples: Generic 'privacy' or 'cybersecurity' with no thread named
'Your work on privacy-preserving machine learning / differential privacy / federated learning' (not a focus)
'Your work on training-data memorization' (the position papers argue the field over-focuses on it)
Describing her as an ML or NLP researcher without the human-centered framing
Attributing a co-authored paper's lead role to Prof. Li when another student led it, in a way that matters to the claim (e.g., 'your benchmark' is fine; inventing findings is not)
Inventing a paper, result, number, or project not in the snapshot
Treating Khoury-profile 'accessibility and fairness for developers' as a current research thread

accurate_connections: T4: inference and data aggregation as understudied harms; re-identification from anonymized data — closest match to Morgan's mobility-data observation
T1: users' mental models of what they disclose to chatbots ('It's a Fair Game'); user-led data minimization (Rescriber)
traps: Leading with 'ML' or 'data science' as the bridge
Connecting via forecasting or mobility data as a research topic
Claiming Morgan has done re-identification research

accurate_connections: T3: perceived control and trust under agent autonomy and personalization — close to Riley's 'do people feel they have a say'
T5: PrivacyMotiv targets UX practitioners — relevant to Riley's product/UX setting
T2: human oversight of AI agents (adjacent)
traps: Rewriting Riley's interest as 'privacy' to match
